summary: Documents the use of DHCP option codes 208 to 211 by PXELINUX, a network boot loader. These codes carry settings that tell the boot loader how to find its configuration. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: When a computer starts up from the network, it asks for directions. This describes four special notes in the answer that one boot program uses to find what to do next.

questions: what is the pxelinux magic option
subtitle: Special DHCP options that configure a network boot loader.

tldr.problem: Network boot loaders need a way to receive configuration from DHCP servers without expecting those options beforehand.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5071 documents four DHCP option codes (208-211) that PXELINUX uses: a magic number to identify valid options, a configuration file path, a path prefix, and a reboot timeout.
tldr.outcome: These options became officially assigned to PXELINUX to avoid conflicts with other uses of those codes in the 'site local' option space.

today: RFC 5071 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. PXELINUX remains a widely used network boot loader, though the MAGIC option (208) is deprecated; future versions of PXELINUX may not check it.

sections.title: Network Boot Configuration
sections.content:
PXE is a firmware-based bootloader that runs on client machines before the operating system loads. It performs a DHCP request to obtain an IP address, then loads a second-stage bootstrap program like PXELINUX. PXELINUX is that second-stage bootloader, which reads DHCP options to configure itself and find kernel images or boot configurations to load.

The problem is that PXE does not know PXELINUX will be used when it requests an IP address, so it cannot ask the DHCP server for the options PXELINUX needs. Local administrators must manually configure their DHCP servers to provide these options anyway. RFC 5071 documents four option codes (208-211) that PXELINUX uses, assigning them officially to avoid conflicts.
sections.plainLanguage: When you boot a computer from the network, the first stage asks for directions. The second stage needs special messages that the first stage did not ask for. This RFC says which message numbers are okay to use for that.

sections.title: The Four DHCP Options
sections.content:
PXELINUX uses four option codes. Option 208 is a MAGIC field containing the bytes 0xF1, 0x00, 0x74, 0x7E. When PXELINUX sees this magic value, it knows the other three options are meant for it. Without this check, PXELINUX might misinterpret options intended for other purposes.

Option 209 is the Configuration File: a filename (in ASCII text) that PXELINUX fetches via TFTP. This file contains further boot-time configuration such as which kernel to load, boot flags and menu text.

Option 210 is the Path Prefix: an ASCII string that is prepended to the configuration filename and to any file paths mentioned inside the configuration file. This lets administrators configure the directory prefix separately from individual filenames.

Option 211 is the Reboot Time: a 32-bit number of seconds. If PXELINUX cannot reach its TFTP server within this time, it reboots. A value of zero disables this timeout, leaving the system waiting for operator intervention. The default timeout is 300 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four special instructions. The first is a magic code that says 'yes, these are for me'. The next three tell the bootloader where to find its configuration file, what folder to look in, and how long to wait before giving up.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
When PXE starts and requests a DHCP lease, the server can provide these four options even though PXE did not ask for them. PXELINUX then loads from the information in the DHCP response and the earlier PXE DHCP lease. It checks for the MAGIC option; if the value matches 0xF1:00:74:7E, it reads the configuration file, prepending the path prefix option if present. It loads images via TFTP according to the configuration.

Throughout this process, PXELINUX counts the time elapsed. If it exceeds the reboot time (option 211), the system reboots, starting the boot process again. This is useful in environments where the boot server might be temporarily unavailable or where an unattended machine needs recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: The bootloader reads the four options in order: it checks the magic number, then loads the config file from the path prefix, and it resets if it takes too long.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content:
RFC 5071 warns that PXE and PXELINUX allow any DHCP server to execute code on a client system. No PXE implementation known at the time implemented authentication, so a client cannot verify it is receiving legitimate configuration from an authorized server.

TFTP also lacks cryptographic signatures, so an attacker on the network path could feed the client forged boot images. Ethernet MAC addresses are used as client identity, so an attacker who spoofs a MAC address can trick a DHCP server into providing that client's credentials and boot images.

The RFC recommends using network firewalls to restrict PXE and PXELINUX traffic to trusted networks. The reboot timeout option itself could be misused to cause a denial-of-service attack on DHCP servers if an attacker forces many clients to reboot repeatedly.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone with access to the network can tell the bootloader to load anything. There is no way to check if a DHCP server is trustworthy. So boot servers should be kept on private, protected networks.
